analysis.one_liner: Cuts the estate tax: 45% top rate, first $10 million tax-free, and quintuples the annual gift exclusion.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote and died when the 107th Congress ended; Congress cut the estate tax that year through the separate H.R. 1836 tax law instead.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have sharply cut the federal estate and gift taxes. The top rate would drop to 45%, the first $10 million of an estate would be exempt from tax, and the amount one person can give another each year tax-free would rise from $10,000 to $50,000, adjusted for inflation. The changes would apply to deaths and gifts after December 31, 2000.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to multimillion-dollar estates. Under the law in effect in 2001, the unified credit already wiped out the estate tax for estates up to $675,000, so raising the exemption to $10 million and cutting the top rate to 45% would benefit only—and most of all—the very largest estates. Wealthy gift-givers would also gain from a fivefold larger annual tax-free gift exclusion, letting them move large sums to heirs during life without triggering gift tax.

how_it_helps.text: It cuts the top estate and gift tax rate from 55% to 45%, lowering the tax on the largest taxable estates.

It replaces the unified credit with a $10 million exemption amount, meaning an estate's tax is computed only on the value above $10 million — under 2001 law the credit shielded far less, so estates between roughly $675,000 and $10 million would owe nothing.
It raises the annual tax-free gift exclusion from $10,000 to $50,000 per recipient, with inflation indexing, letting wealthy families transfer more to heirs during life tax-free.
The cuts apply retroactively, to estates of people dying and gifts made after December 31, 2000.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury — and ultimately all taxpayers — through the lost revenue. The estate tax was paid by only a small fraction of the largest estates, so the bill's benefits would be concentrated among the wealthiest families while the cost is spread across everyone who relies on federal services or shares the debt burden.

drawbacks.text: The bill is a tax cut aimed almost entirely at the largest estates: because the existing credit already exempted estates up to $675,000, a $10 million exemption provides nothing to most families and its full value goes to multimillion-dollar estates.
The lost estate and gift tax revenue would have to be made up by other taxpayers, through higher taxes elsewhere, reduced federal services, or larger deficits.

A much larger annual gift exclusion ($50,000 per recipient) mainly helps families wealthy enough to give away large sums each year, and makes it easier to move wealth out of the taxable estate during life.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but narrow: they flow to heirs of very large estates and to wealthy gift-givers, while the cost — lost federal revenue — is spread across everyone. An honest supporter would frame this as relief for family farms and businesses facing estate taxes, but the bill's $10 million exemption goes far beyond that, shielding estates of that size entirely. There is no offsetting benefit in the bill for middle- or working-income families.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died without a vote when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Mac Collins introduced the bill on April 4, 2001, with three Republican cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day.

The bill never received a committee markup or a floor vote; its complete action history consists of the introduction, referral, the sponsor's remarks, and an August 2001 entry pointing to H.R. 1836, the broad 2001 tax cut bill that carried that year's estate tax changes.

H.R. 1836 — the Economic Growth and Tax Relief Reconciliation Act of 2001 — was enacted that June and included a phased reduction and temporary repeal of the estate tax, so the direction of policy moved the way this bill wanted even though the bill itself never advanced.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large estates came out ahead despite the bill's death: Congress enacted a separate estate tax cut in 2001 through H.R. 1836, the bill this one pointed to. No one lost anything from this bill's failure, since it never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large estates, via the separate 2001 tax law

for.name: Rep. Mac Collins
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Estate Tax Relief Act of 2001 and made introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 3 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Reps. Norwood, Deal of Georgia, and Chambliss).

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no party split is recorded; all four sponsors and cosponsors were Georgia Republicans, and no Democrat ever signed on.

industries.industry: Very wealthy households and large estates
industries.note: A $10 million exemption and 45% top rate would eliminate the estate tax for estates under $10 million and cut it sharply above that, with the largest dollar benefits going to the biggest fortunes. The bill contained nothing for families whose estates never came near the tax, while the lost revenue would be borne by everyone.

industries.industry: Estate planning lawyers and wealth advisors
industries.note: A $10 million exemption would remove nearly all estates from tax planning, cutting demand for estate-planning work. The larger gift exclusion, however, would create new planning work around lifetime gifts.

Estate tax relief is typically promoted as protection for family farms and businesses that are asset-rich but cash-poor. Under this bill they would pay nothing, though under the pre-2001 credit and existing special rules most already faced little or no estate tax.
